title: Mercury delay-line revival: recirculating photonic loop broadcasts streaming weights
idea: Replace the 1940s mercury tank with a ~2 m low-loss silicon-nitride spiral on the interposer (~10 ns, 64 wavelengths x 50 Gb/s) closed by an SOA regenerator; a weight tile read once from HBM recirculates for N laps and 8-16 compute chiplets tap it each lap via ring drop filters.
why: Facts 5/8: each weight byte crosses the HBM PHY once instead of once per consumer or per micro-batch step, cutting DRAM reads and pJ/bit on broadcast/expert-shared traffic ~4-8x; loop holds only ~32 kbit so it is a broadcast medium with temporal reuse, not a store.

title: Drum-memory revival: command-free rotational streaming mode for HBM stacks
idea: Add a 'drum mode' in which each bank activates rows in a fixed cyclic order and streams them past the PHY like drum tracks past fixed heads, with no command/address traffic; a compiler places tensors at rotational offsets (IBM 650 SOAP-style optimum programming) so data arrives exactly when compute needs it.
why: Facts 3/7/8: drops C/A pins and scheduler logic (~15-20% of PHY area/power), every opened row is fully consumed (no 128x overfetch) for streaming AI loads, and refresh becomes implicit because every row is read once per rotation inside the retention window.

title: Bubble-memory rotating field shifts data through stacks without wires
idea: As bubble memory moved every bubble with one rotating in-plane field, wrap a two-phase package coil around a stack of dies carrying permalloy T-bar/chevron domain-propagation tracks, so one resonant global field shifts data from every tier toward a port die at once, crossing tiers by magnetostatic coupling through thin bond layers.
why: Facts 5/6: per-wire CV^2 switching is replaced by one shared field whose energy is recovered in a high-Q LC tank, and no TSVs are needed for bulk sequential transfer; claimed 3-5x lower movement energy if massive parallelism compensates for MHz-class shift rates.

title: Plated-wire looms weave copper interposer fabric instead of silicon CoWoS
idea: Revive the 1960s plated-wire memory weaving looms to weave 15-25 um insulated copper wires at ~40 um pitch into a fabric that is laminated into an organic panel and laser-opened at die sites, forming long memory-to-logic links.
why: Fact 6 and capital: silicon-interposer (CoWoS) capacity is a chokepoint; woven round wire has ~10x lower resistance per mm than 1 um RDL, so HBM can sit 20-50 mm away (more stacks per GPU) on loom-class capital (~$1M) instead of a fab line.

title: Core-rope wired-sum: shared magnetic cores reduce partial sums in-package
idea: Like Apollo rope memory threading dozens of wires through one core, route the current-mode outputs of 8-16 processing-in-memory chiplets through shared thin-film magnetic cores on the substrate, so one secondary winding carries the analog sum and a single host ADC reads the reduced value.
why: Fact 5: in-package accumulate/all-reduce of partial dot products moves one value instead of N (8-16x less reduction traffic) with zero active circuitry; precision ~6-8 bits, limited by core linearity and drive matching.

title: 1950s ferroelectric matrix switches remap failed HBM dies after bonding
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1952 BaTiO3 ferroelectric matrix as HZO ferroelectric-FET crosspoint switches in the HBM base die that nonvolatilely reroute channels and TSV groups around a dead core die or bad TSV cluster after stacking, holding state with zero power.
why: Fact 6: much of HBM's 20-30% yield loss arises at stack/bond level; post-bond repair could recover roughly half of it (~10-15% more sellable stacks per wafer start) with negligible area.

title: Goto parametron revival: phase-encoded links pumped by shared resonant clock
idea: Each link endpoint is a varactor parametric oscillator pumped at 2f by a package-wide resonant LC clock grid; a bit is the 0 or pi phase of the subharmonic oscillation, seeded by a tiny injection and amplified by pump energy, so there is no rail-to-rail driver.
why: Facts 5/10: sidesteps the CV^2 voltage floor because signal energy circulates in high-Q resonators and is mostly recovered; target <0.1 pJ/bit for die-to-die links versus ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit for today's parallel D2D PHYs.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode repeaters turn passive interposers into regenerating links
idea: Deposit two-terminal Esaki/backward tunnel diodes every few mm along passive interposer wires; their negative-resistance bistability latches and re-sharpens 50-100 mV signals using only a shared bias line, with no transistors in the interposer.
why: Facts 5/10: permits ~70 mV signaling over 20-40 mm interposer runs (realistic 5-10x lower wire energy than full swing) while keeping the interposer a cheap passive part; extends HBM reach so more stacks fit per accelerator.

title: Cryotron-era cryo pods: LN2-cooled HBM with superconducting YBCO flex links
idea: Revive 1950s-80s cryogenic computing pragmatically: run memory stacks at 77 K in liquid-nitrogen pods (no helium) where DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude and copper resistance falls ~7x, and connect them to warm compute through YBCO coated-conductor flex cables.
why: Facts 3/5: refresh nearly vanishes (retention seconds to hours), wire energy and IR drop shrink, and lossless flex lets large pooled stacks sit 0.5-1 m from compute; avoids the Qatar helium chokepoint by using LN2.

title: CCD memory revival: bucket-brigade charge conveyors replace HBM global datalines
idea: Build buried-channel CCD lanes in the HBM core and base dies that shift whole rows of charge packets from banks to the PHY with three-phase resonant clocks, sensing only at the lane end, instead of precharging and swinging long global I/O lines.
why: Facts 5/7/8: charge packets move at ~0.1-0.2 V signal levels with recoverable clock energy, claimed 3-5x less on-die data-path energy (about half of HBM pJ/bit) and a smaller periphery.

title: Tape-library robots shuttle preloaded CXL memory sleds between racks
idea: Treat DRAM like 1960s tape reels: a robotic library moves hot-pluggable 1-4 TB CXL memory sleds, preloaded with model weights or KV caches, to whichever rack needs them and inserts them into blind-mate CXL backplane slots in seconds.
why: Scarce-resource strategy: fleet DRAM utilization is often <50%; migrating physical capacity on minute timescales instead of over-provisioning every server could cut fleet DRAM 20-30%, and preloaded sleds avoid pushing TBs over the network.

title: Pupin loading coils make interposer wires distortionless Heaviside lines
idea: Add periodic thin-film CoZrTa-cored inductors along RC-dominated interposer and RDL wires, as Pupin loaded telephone lines, pushing them toward Heaviside's distortionless condition so pulses keep their shape without CTLE/DFE equalizers.
why: Facts 5/6: longer HBM-to-logic reach at low swing without power-hungry equalization, ~30-50% PHY energy savings and more stacks per package; inductor area and loss at GHz are the risk.

title: Theremin passive cavity bug revived as backscatter memory chiplets
idea: Like the 1945 Great Seal bug that transmitted with no internal power, memory chiplets carry a resonant slot antenna loaded by a varactor; the host floods the package with a 140-300 GHz carrier and reads data from the modulated reflections.
why: Fact 5: link power moves to one efficient host-side source, memory-side transmit energy <0.05 pJ/bit, and read paths need no metallurgical bond, so chiplets become wireless and easily reworked.

title: Holographic-memory optics revived: volume-hologram lid routes chiplet beams
idea: Revive 1960s-70s holographic page-memory optics as interconnect: memory dies emit page-wide micro-LED/VCSEL arrays upward and a volume hologram in the package lid diffracts each beam to a fixed photodiode on any of several compute chiplets, giving all-to-all fan-out without waveguide routing.
why: Facts 5/6: thousands of 5-10 Gb/s optical channels per mm^2 with no interposer wiring, ~1 pJ/bit, and broadcast fan-out for free.

title: Ethernet vampire-tap revival: coupler-tapped multidrop buses restore channel capacity
idea: Like 10BASE5 taps on one coax, hang 4-8 memory modules on a single terminated backplane line through contactless directional couplers instead of stubs, so taps do not reflect and the bus stays clean at high data rates.
why: Capacity/supply: high-speed DDR5 allows only 1-2 DIMMs per channel; coupler buses could restore 4-8, letting servers use many cheaper lower-density parts from older, available nodes instead of scarce 64-128 GB RDIMMs.

title: Telephone-hybrid revival: simultaneous bidirectional signaling doubles every TSV
idea: Revive the telephone 2-wire/4-wire hybrid and Edison's quadruplex telegraph: each TSV and microbump carries read and write data at once, and an on-die replica-driver hybrid subtracts the local transmit waveform from the received sum.
why: Fact 6: halves TSV/bump count per unit bandwidth (or doubles stack bandwidth), shrinking the TSV area tax that makes HBM ~3x the wafer area per bit; ~10-15% die area back.

title: Phantom-circuit revival: center-tapped third channel rides two differential pairs
idea: Like 1880s telephone phantom circuits, encode a third data stream as the common-mode difference between two differential pairs, injected and recovered through center-tapped terminations, on memory SerDes and package traces.
why: 1.5x bandwidth per wire on differential memory links (CXL/SerDes), so fewer package pins and substrate layers per TB/s; modest energy overhead, common-mode noise is the risk.

title: Morse-code revival: frequency-weighted transition-minimal codes on memory links
idea: As Morse gave frequent letters the shortest codes, profile tensor statistics (BF16/FP8 exponent clusters, zero runs) and assign link codewords so the commonest symbols cause the fewest wire toggles and terminated ones, with codebooks swapped per tensor in the PHY.
why: Fact 5: I/O energy tracks toggles and terminated ones; skewed AI tensors allow 30-50% fewer transitions (30-50% lower link energy) plus ~1.3x effective bandwidth from compression.

title: Goodyear STARAN revival: multidimensional-access memory serves bit-planes on demand
idea: Revive STARAN's 1972 multi-dimensional-access memory: a flip-network permutation in the HBM base die lets one stored array be read word-wise or bit-plane-wise, so precision-adaptive kernels fetch only the top k bit-planes of weights or activations.
why: Facts 5/8: fetching 4 of 16 bit-planes moves 4x fewer bits for draft, speculative or early-exit passes, without storing duplicate low-precision copies (saves capacity too).

title: Setun balanced-ternary revival: end-to-end trits for ternary-weight models
idea: Revive the 1958 Setun balanced-ternary computer as a data path: store {-1,0,+1} weights as three charge levels (VDD/2 +/- dV) in DRAM cells, ship them over PAM-3 lanes without binary conversion, and sense them with a ternary sense amplifier.
why: Density/movement: 1.58 bits per cell versus 2-bit packing that wastes ~21%, and ternary-weight LLMs cut traffic ~10x versus FP16; end-to-end trits capture it with no unpack logic.

title: Differential-analyzer revival: ship activations between dies as analog charge
idea: Revive analog computing: between a processing-in-memory die and the logic die, send each 6-bit activation as one analog charge sample per wire per transfer, consumed directly by an analog MAC on the far side with no ADC/DAC pair.
why: Fact 5: ~6x fewer transfers per value and link energy per value near one-bit energy; inference tolerates ~1% analog error, but noise and calibration are the risk.

title: Williams-tube revival: electron beams cross a vacuum gap between dies
idea: Revive the CRT storage tube's beam principle with on-chip field-emitter arrays (Spindt or CNT tips) on the memory die firing modulated electron beams across a sealed 5-20 um vacuum gap onto collector pads on the facing logic die, with no metallurgical bond.
why: Fact 6: ballistic transport into tiny collector capacitance with no TSV or bump, potentially >100 GHz per channel, and stacks become reworkable; vacuum sealing and emitter lifetime are speculative.

title: Marconi coherer revival: link receivers that latch arriving bits nonvolatilely
idea: Like the 1890s coherer whose filings fused under RF, end each die-to-die write lane with a filamentary Ag/Cu nanogap switch that forms a filament when a pulse arrives, so the receiver is itself a nonvolatile staging latch, reset later by a counter-pulse 'tapper'.
why: Facts 3/5: merges receiver and write buffer, removing an SRAM/register staging hop for write-mostly streams (checkpoints, KV-cache spill), ~30% data-path energy on those writes; endurance limits it to staging, not working memory.

title: Core-memory ferrite rings replace TSVs as fluorine-free inductive stack vias
idea: Revive core memory's transformer coupling: each thinned die carries thin-film coils around sputtered NiZn/NiFe ferrite ring segments aligned through the stack, so flux threads 4-8 dies like wires through a core and carries data with no holes etched.
why: Constraint: removes Bosch DRIE (SF6/C4F8) TSV etch and HF post-cleans entirely; the ferrite core concentrates flux so coils shrink ~3x versus air-core inductive links, raising channel density and cutting the HBM TSV area/yield tax (fact 6).

title: Sun proximity-communication revival: capacitive face-to-face HBM with no bumps
idea: Revive Sun Microsystems' abandoned proximity communication: memory and logic dies overlap face-to-face with 10-20 um pads coupled capacitively across a 1-3 um plain SiO2 gap, clamped mechanically, with electronic pad steering cancelling misalignment.
why: Constraint: no underfill, fluoropolymer adhesive, plating or fluorinated etch; dies stay reworkable so known-good stacks replace bad ones (fact 6 yield), at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit and 10k+ channels/mm^2.

title: Photophone revival: infrared micro-LEDs signal straight through thinned silicon stacks
idea: Like Bell's 1880 photophone sending speech on light, place 1.3-1.55 um InGaAs micro-LEDs on one die and Ge photodiodes on dies above; silicon is transparent at these wavelengths, so data crosses several thinned dies vertically with no via.
why: Constraint: no TSV etch and no fluorinated plasma or cleans; hundreds of vertical channels per stack at ~1 pJ/bit decouple stack bandwidth from TSV yield (fact 6).

title: Acoustic delay-line revival: AlN gigahertz ultrasound bus through the stack
idea: Revive the delay line's acoustic signaling: sputtered AlN transducers (not PVDF fluoropolymer piezo) launch 5-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses that travel vertically through bonded silicon tiers to receivers on every die, forming a broadcast command/address and refresh-control bus.
why: Constraint: AlN and direct silicon bonding need no fluorinated films or TSVs; removes the C/A TSV bundle (~10-20% of TSVs) and gives free broadcast to all tiers at a few Gb/s per transducer.

title: Bell Labs beam-lead revival: cantilevered gold beams tile dies interposer-free
idea: Revive Lepselter's 1960s beam-lead process: gold beams plated on the die are released by a KOH/TMAH back-etch through a laser-ablated hard mask (no HF, no fluorine plasma) to cantilever 50-100 um past the edge, then thermocompression-bonded to neighboring memory and logic dies.
why: Constraint and capital: avoids the silicon interposer's fluorine-based DRIE and the CoWoS bottleneck; 10 um-pitch edge beams give ~100 lanes per mm of die edge, enough for wide memory links at low cost.

title: Tape-automated-bonding revival: folded polyimide tapes stack DRAM without TSVs
idea: Revive 1970s reel-to-reel TAB: DRAM dies are inner-lead-bonded to non-fluorinated PMDA-ODA polyimide tape with 20 um-pitch copper leads, and the tape is accordion-folded so 8-16 dies stack with their leads converging on a base die.
why: Constraint: copper/polyimide/gold TAB uses no PTFE, fluorinated polyimide or fluorine etch and no TSVs; roll-to-roll throughput gives HBM-like stacks at near-LPDDR cost (~10x cheaper per stack, lower bandwidth).

title: Cordwood-module revival: edge-standing DRAM dies plug into logic like books
idea: Revive Apollo-era cordwood construction: thinned DRAM dies with I/O routed to one edge stand perpendicular to the logic die like books on a shelf, their laser-diced edge pads finished with PFAS-free electroless Ni/Au and joined to a grid of landing pads.
why: Constraint: no TSV etch or fluorinated plating additives; each die gets its own full-edge I/O (10 mm x 25 pads/mm = 250+ signals) instead of sharing through-stack vias, and coolant can flow between the 'books'.

title: IBM TCM revival: glass-ceramic cofired substrates replace silicon interposers
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s thermal conduction module substrate: 30-60-layer cofired glass-ceramic/copper panels, screen-printed with Cu paste and mechanically punched 50 um vias, carrying many HBM-class stacks plus logic over 100-150 mm.
why: Constraint: punching, screen printing and cofiring use no photoresist PAGs, HF or fluorinated plasma; breaks the CoWoS chokepoint on US-buildable 1980s-class tooling, with 15-20 um lines fine for wide, slower memory channels.

title: IBM EL-1 revival: maskless e-beam RDL in non-fluorinated PMMA resist
idea: Revive IBM's 1970s EL-1 direct-write e-beam personalization: multi-beam writers pattern interposer RDL and base-die customization layers directly in PMMA or HSQ, with no PFAS photoacid generators, giving per-product memory interface variants without masks.
why: Constraint: removes chemically amplified resists with PFAS PAGs; capital: no $1-5M mask sets for low-volume custom HBM base dies and interposers, and throughput suffices for a few coarse layers.

title: Xerography revival: electrophotographic copper-toner printing of package wiring
idea: Revive Carlson's 1938 xerography: a laser-imaged photoconductor drum picks up charged copper-nanoparticle toner and transfers it to the package substrate, followed by sintering and electroless copper thickening, giving maskless, resist-free 10-20 um RDL.
why: Constraint: no photoresist at all, so no PFAS PAGs or fluorosurfactants; a printer-class tool (~$1M) replaces lithography for package redistribution, cutting capital and enabling distributed US packaging.

title: 1968 ECDM revival: spark-drilled glass interposer vias in caustic, no HF
idea: Revive Kurafuji's electrochemical discharge machining: tool electrodes in NaOH/KOH electrolyte create gas-film sparks that thermally and chemically drill 20-50 um vias through glass interposer panels, with arrays of parallel electrodes for throughput.
why: Constraint: removes hydrofluoric acid (laser-induced deep etching) and SF6 plasma from glass via formation, unlocking large, cheap, low-loss glass panels that host many HBM stacks.

title: Trench-DRAM revival: HBr/Cl2 deep-trench etch makes fluorine-free TSVs
idea: Repurpose the abandoned IBM/Siemens/Qimonda trench-capacitor deep-silicon etch (HBr/O2/Cl2, AR ~50:1) to etch 5 x 30 um TSVs in thinned DRAM, with SiBrxOy sidewall passivation in place of Bosch fluorocarbon polymer.
why: Constraint: TSVs without SF6 (the strongest greenhouse gas) or PFAS-class C4F8, reusing existing deep-trench know-how; slower (~1 um/min) etch is the cost, offset by thinner dies (fact 6).

title: 1980s DNQ-novolac i-line strategy for PFAS-free domestic interposers
idea: Standardize HBM interposers and RDL at >=1.5-2 um lines on non-chemically-amplified DNQ-novolac resist and i-line steppers, 1980s tooling that is cheap, available used and buildable in the U.S., and design memory interfaces wide and slow enough to fit those rules.
why: Constraint and US manufacturability: DNQ resists contain no PFAS PAGs; i-line steppers cost ~$3-5M versus $20M+ for ArF, enabling domestic interposer capacity under a shared open standard.

title: Vacuum-tube mica revival: muscovite sheets as PTFE-free high-speed dielectric
idea: Revive mica, the dielectric of early capacitors and tube spacers: cleave natural muscovite to 10-25 um sheets and laminate it with copper by adhesive-free thermocompression as the high-speed layers for memory-to-logic package traces.
why: Constraint: replaces PTFE-based laminates used for >50 GHz links; mica has tan-delta ~0.0002 and atomically flat surfaces for fine lines, and is mined in the U.S. (North Carolina) and India.

title: Air-bridge revival: suspended interposer wires via polynorbornene thermal burnout
idea: Revive 1970s GaAs MMIC air-bridges: pattern interposer signal lines over sacrificial polynorbornene that decomposes at ~400 C and diffuses out through a thin SiN cap, leaving lines suspended in air (k~1).
why: Constraint: replaces fluorinated low-k (FSG) and HF-vapor release; wire capacitance falls ~3-4x, cutting interposer link energy ~2-3x (fact 5) and extending HBM reach.

title: Cray-2 immersion revival with ester fluids enables taller HBM stacks
idea: Revive the Cray-2's total-immersion cooling but swap Fluorinert for natural or synthetic ester dielectric fluid, with micro-jets aimed through the gaps between stacks and a passive thermosiphon loop, removing heat through stack sidewalls.
why: Constraint: no PFAS coolants (Fluorinert/Novec production has been exited); side-cooling relieves the thermal cap on stack height so 16-24-high stacks run unthrottled, ~50% more GB per footprint.

title: Bell WT4 revival: polyethylene millimeter-wave waveguides carry rack memory traffic
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1970s WT4 millimeter waveguide as HDPE or polystyrene dielectric waveguides (not PTFE) at 130-300 GHz, driven by CMOS mm-wave transceivers on CXL memory sleds and linking pooled memory 1-5 m to compute.
why: Constraint: avoids PTFE dielectric and fluoropolymer cable jackets; ~1-2 pJ/bit and lower cost than optics at rack reach makes memory pooling cheap enough to raise utilization.

title: Chappe optical-telegraph revival: steerable free-space links to memory pools
idea: Revive Chappe's line-of-sight optical telegraph inside the data hall: MEMS-steered free-space optical transceivers on rack tops form a reconfigurable mesh to pooled memory racks and are re-aimed in milliseconds as jobs move.
why: Constraint: no fluoropolymer (FEP) plenum cable jackets or fluorine-doped fiber; direct reconfigurable circuits to memory pools with no packet switches, raising pooled DRAM utilization ~20-30%.

title: Ferreed-switch revival: magnetically latched crosspoints circuit-switch pooled memory
idea: Revive Bell's 1960s ferreed (remanent-magnet-latched reed switch from No. 1 ESS) as MEMS crosspoint arrays with semi-hard magnetic latches that connect any server's copper lanes to any memory sled and hold with zero power.
why: Constraint: glass-sealed NiFe reeds need no fluorinated chemistry or fluoropolymer insulation; circuit switching adds no per-access latency or energy (just a wire) versus 100+ ns and several pJ/bit through CXL packet switches.

title: Core-weaving revival: robots thread insulated microwire through laser-drilled stacks
idea: Like core-memory weavers threading wires through ferrite rings, laser-ablate aligned 20 um holes through a stack of thinned dies or glass and robotically thread polyester-imide-enamelled (not PTFE) copper microwire through them, then press-contact it to pads on each tier.
why: Constraint: laser ablation plus threading replaces Bosch DRIE, PFAS resists and plating chemistry for vertical interconnect; suited to 4-8-tier power/ground and slower signals at very low capital.

title: Single-wire earth-return revival: bulk silicon as shared stack return path
idea: Revive the telegraph's single-wire earth return: use the heavily doped bulk of ohmically bonded dies as the common signal and power return, so the stack needs signal vias only, not paired ground vias.
why: Constraint: halving vertical via count halves the slower fluorine-free (HBr/laser) via process time, making it economic; shrinks the HBM TSV area tax (fact 6) ~30-40%, with substrate noise the main risk.

title: Spark-gap revival: impulse radio broadcasts between chiplets inside package cavity
idea: Revive spark-gap carrierless transmission as on-chip impulse UWB: memory chiplets radiate 20-50 ps pulses from on-die antennas into the metal-lid cavity, and compute chiplets receive with crystal-set-style envelope detectors (no PLL or LO).
why: Constraint: wireless links need no TSVs, no fluorinated etch and no PTFE high-frequency substrate; broadcast fan-out of weights is free at ~1-3 pJ/bit and 10-20 Gb/s per channel.

title: Hollerith tabulator revival: spring pins in low-melt cups socket HBM
idea: Revive Hollerith's 1890 tabulator contacts, pins dipping through holes into mercury cups, with Field's-metal (Bi-In-Sn, 62 C melt) micro-cups on the substrate that receive HBM stack pins, making stacks socketed, flux-free and reworkable.
why: Constraint: no fluorinated no-clean fluxes or fluoropolymer underfill; one bad HBM stack is swapped instead of scrapping a $10k+ module (fact 6 yield), raising effective HBM supply ~5-10%.
